vignette:
The Weight of Water

Raymond is a 74-year-old man who has spent the better part of four decades tutoring secondary school students in mathematics and French. He is precise by nature — a man who finds comfort in the orderly logic of equations and conjugation tables. He lives with his partner of twelve years, Elspeth, in a modest stone cottage in the Scottish Borders, and until three years ago, he describes his life as having settled into a rhythm that suited him well.

In the autumn of 2021, catastrophic flooding swept through the valley where Raymond and Elspeth live. What began as a weather warning on a Tuesday evening became, by Wednesday morning, something Raymond could not have prepared himself for. The river behind their property burst its banks before dawn. He remembers standing in the hallway in his dressing gown, watching dark water pour under the front door and rise across the flagstone floor with a speed and indifference that he still cannot fully articulate. He and Elspeth made it to the upper floor, but they remained stranded there for nearly eleven hours, listening to the water move through their home below — furniture shifting, glass breaking, the low groan of the house absorbing what it could not stop. Raymond tells it quietly, but his hands press flat against his thighs as he speaks.

The water eventually receded. Their home was gutted. They stayed with Elspeth's daughter for four months during the repairs. Raymond returned to his tutoring work almost immediately, partly out of financial necessity and partly, he admits, because sitting with students and working through problems gave him something to focus on that had edges and solutions. But he found himself struggling in ways he had not anticipated. He began arriving to sessions having slept only a few hours, waking most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart pounding, certain he can hear water — pipes, rain against the window, a tap left running. He lies still and listens until he is sure.

Rain has become a source of dread. On overcast days, Raymond checks the weather application on his phone compulsively, sometimes a dozen times before noon. When it does rain heavily, he finds it nearly impossible to concentrate. Twice he has cancelled tutoring sessions during storms, telling students he was unwell. He feels ashamed of this. He describes himself as a man who has always been dependable, and the gap between who he was and who he feels himself to be now sits heavily with him.

His relationship with Elspeth, though fundamentally solid, has become quietly strained. She weathered the flood alongside him and has, by Raymond's account, largely moved forward. He loves her and does not want to burden her, so he says little about the nights he cannot sleep, or the afternoons when he sits in his car after a tutoring session and cannot immediately bring himself to drive home past the river. He takes the long road now, adding fifteen minutes to every journey.

There are moments during sessions — particularly when a student is struggling and Raymond is trying to hold his patience and his focus — when the flood returns to him without warning. Not as a thought, but as a sensation: the cold of the water around his ankles, the particular smell of it, the sound of Elspeth calling his name from the top of the stairs. He blinks, reorients himself, returns to the problem on the page. The student rarely notices. Raymond notices everything.

He came to therapy, he says, because Elspeth finally asked him to. He had not told her the half of it, but she had seen enough. He sat in the first session with his hands folded and his posture very straight, and said that he was not sure he had anything worth complaining about — they had survived, after all, and the house had been repaired. He said this with complete sincerity, and with eyes that were already tired before the session had properly begun.
